result: The crystal structure of human Importin-9 bound to full-length X. laevis H2A-H2B was solved to 2.7 Å resolution. Importin-9 consists of 20 tandem HEAT repeats forming a superhelical structure with a mostly acidic concave surface that wraps around H2A-H2B, burying 1352 Å² (26% of H2A-H2B surface) at three distinct interfaces. The H2A-H2B dimer maintains its canonical histone-fold structure (r.m.s.d. 0.505 Å with nucleosomal H2A-H2B), while the N- and C-terminal tails of both histones and portions of Importin-9 (first 14 residues and H19loop) were not modeled due to missing electron density.
evaluation: The structural determination is well-supported by crystallographic data at 2.7 Å resolution (C125), with detailed descriptions of the HEAT repeat architecture (C1-C2), surface properties (C3), and interface characteristics (C4-C6). The structural alignment with nucleosomal H2A-H2B provides quantitative validation (C7-C8), and the identification of disordered regions is appropriately based on missing electron density (C9-C12). The resolution is adequate for the level of structural detail described.

result: Interface 1 between Importin-9 and H2A-H2B comprises the loop following helix 2B and the last turns of helices 3B, 4B, and 5B of Importin-9, which interact with α2-L2-α3 of H2A and α1-L1-α2 of H2B. These histone regions constitute a significant portion of the basic DNA-binding surface found in nucleosomes. The interface involves hydrogen-bonding that caps the C-terminal ends of Importin-9 B helices, including notable end-to-end capping of Importin-9 helix 4B by H2B helix α2. Despite electrostatic complementarity, the interface also employs many hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and main chain interactions.
evaluation: The detailed structural characterization of Interface 1 is well-supported by crystallographic data (C13-C15) with specific structural features described. The functional significance is appropriately inferred by comparison to nucleosome structure (C16-C17), and the diverse nature of interactions is documented (C18). The claims are consistent with the resolution of the structure and supported by referenced figures.

result: Interface 2 involves Importin-9 helices 7B, 8B, and the H8loop binding to the short 28KKRRK32 segment of the H2B N-terminal tail. The electron density for these H2B residues is weak and B-factors are high (>100 Å²), suggesting dynamic interactions. The interface involves both electrostatic interactions between charged H2B side chains and acidic Importin-9 residues, as well as hydrophobic interactions involving the aliphatic parts of basic side chains and their backbone.
evaluation: The structural characterization of Interface 2 is supported by crystallographic data (C19), with appropriate interpretation of weak electron density and high B-factors as indicators of dynamic interactions (C20-C21). The description of interaction types is consistent with the structural data (C22-C23). The high B-factors (>100 Å²) are appropriately interpreted as evidence for flexibility rather than poor data quality.

result: Interface 3 involves the last three HEAT repeats of Importin-9 (specifically the last turn of helix 18A, the H18-19loop, the C-terminal half of helix 19A, and the first turn of helix 20B) interacting with H2A and H2B. Unusually, charges are reversed at this interface compared to typical importin-cargo interactions, with a basic patch on Importin-9 complementing an acidic surface on the histones. The interface includes notable salt bridges between Importin-9 Arg898 and several acidic H2A residues, many hydrophobic contacts, and hydrogen-bonding that caps several helices.
evaluation: The structural characterization of Interface 3 is well-supported by crystallographic data (C24-C28). The identification of charge reversal is a notable observation supported by electrostatic surface analysis (C25). Specific interactions like the Arg898 salt bridges are appropriately documented (C26), and the diverse nature of interactions is described (C27-C28). The structural details are consistent with the resolution of the structure.

result: Isothermal titration calorimetry experiments demonstrate that Importin-9 binds full-length H2A-H2B with high affinity (KD = 30 nM). Deletion of H2A tails (H2AΔTail-H2B, KD = 40 nM), H2B tail (H2A-H2BΔ(1-35), KD = 40 nM), or both tails (H2AΔTail-H2BΔTail, KD = 40 nM) does not significantly affect binding affinity, consistent with structural observations that these regions are disordered. Deletion of the Importin-9 H8loop also does not decrease binding (KD = 10 nM). However, removal of the H18-19loop reduces affinity 15-fold (KD = 450 nM) with an endothermic binding reaction, suggesting substantial contribution of Interface 3 to total binding energy. Removal of the disordered H19loop does not affect affinity (KD = 40 nM).
evaluation: The binding affinity measurements by ITC are well-documented with appropriate replicates (triplicate experiments) and error analysis (68.3% confidence intervals reported in Table 1). The systematic deletion analysis provides strong evidence that histone tails contribute minimally to binding energy (C29-C36), while Interface 3 (H18-19loop) contributes substantially (C37-C39). The consistency between structural observations (disordered regions) and binding data (no effect of tail deletions) strengthens the conclusions (C31, C33). The endothermic binding upon H18-19loop deletion is an interesting thermodynamic observation (C38).

result: A large portion of the Importin-9 interface on H2A-H2B overlaps with the DNA-binding and H3-H4-binding interfaces used in nucleosomes, a feature common to many H2A-H2B histone chaperones. Importin-9 buries more surface area on H2A-H2B (1352 Å²) than well-characterized histone chaperones including Nap1 (387 Å²), Swr1 (488 Å²), Anp32e (533 Å²), Chz1 (906 Å²), Spt16 of FACT (185 Å²), and YL1 (883 Å²). Gel-shift assays demonstrate that titration of either Nap1 or Importin-9 against DNA•H2A-H2B complexes leads to release of free DNA as the proteins bind H2A-H2B, suggesting that Importin-9 can act as a histone chaperone by shielding H2A-H2B from promiscuous interactions.
evaluation: The comparison of Importin-9 to histone chaperones is well-supported by structural analysis (C42-C44) with quantitative buried surface area measurements from the crystal structure and literature comparisons. The gel-shift assays provide functional evidence for chaperone-like activity (C45-C46), and the interpretation is appropriately cautious (C47). The larger buried surface area compared to known chaperones is a notable observation that strengthens the chaperone hypothesis.

result: Unlike typical importin-cargo complexes, RanGTP does not dissociate the Importin-9•H2A-H2B complex but instead forms a stable heterotetrameric RanGTP•Importin-9•H2A-H2B complex. This was demonstrated by multiple complementary approaches: pull-down assays showing histones remain bound to immobilized Importin-9 even with excess RanGTP (C48-C51), electrophoretic mobility shift assays showing formation of complexes containing equimolar amounts of all three components (C52-C54), size exclusion chromatography (C55), analytical ultracentrifugation showing a 4.6S species consistent with the quaternary complex (C56-C59), and SAXS analysis estimating molecular weight of 161.1 kDa, nearly identical to the expected 163.2 kDa (C60-C61).
evaluation: The formation of the RanGTP•Importin-9•H2A-H2B complex is exceptionally well-supported by multiple orthogonal biophysical techniques (pull-down, EMSA, SEC, AUC, SAXS). The RanGTP used was validated as active by control experiments with Kapβ2 (C49). The convergence of evidence from different methods (sedimentation coefficient 4.6S from AUC, molecular weight 161.1 kDa from SAXS matching expected 163.2 kDa) provides strong support for the quaternary complex stoichiometry. This is a major finding that contradicts the typical importin-cargo-RanGTP behavior.

result: Structural comparisons with six different importin•RanGTP complexes reveal that RanGTP consistently binds at the N-terminal HEAT repeats of importins, with structurally conserved interactions at HEAT repeats 1-4. Structural alignments of Importin-9 HEAT repeats 1-4 with corresponding regions of other importins show r.m.s.d. values ranging from 2.51-5.02 Å, suggesting that the N-terminal HEAT repeats of Importin-9 are likely important for RanGTP binding. This prediction is supported by an Importin-9 mutant lacking HEAT repeats 1-3 that no longer binds RanGTP. The predicted Ran-binding site at the N-terminus of Importin-9 appears separate from but adjacent to the H2A-H2B binding site, suggesting RanGTP can access Importin-9 without dislodging H2A-H2B, though proximity could modulate interactions.
evaluation: The structural prediction of the RanGTP binding site is well-supported by systematic comparison with six importin•RanGTP structures (C62-C70) with quantitative r.m.s.d. values provided. The prediction is experimentally validated by the deletion mutant lacking HEAT repeats 1-3 that cannot bind RanGTP (C72). The inference about spatial separation of binding sites is reasonable based on structural analysis (C73). However, the speculation about modulation of interactions (C75) is appropriately presented as a possibility rather than a conclusion.

result: Native gel-based competition and nucleosome assembly/disassembly assays demonstrate that RanGTP modulates Importin-9-H2A-H2B interactions. DNA cannot compete H2A-H2B from Importin-9•H2A-H2B but can compete H2A-H2B from RanGTP•Importin-9•H2A-H2B to produce Importin-9•RanGTP and DNA•H2A-H2B. Conversely, Importin-9 efficiently displaces DNA from DNA•H2A-H2B complexes, while Importin-9•RanGTP does not. In nucleosome assembly assays, Nap1 and Importin-9•RanGTP can form nucleosomes from tetrasomes, while Importin-9 alone cannot and instead prevents H2A-H2B deposition. Notably, Importin-9•RanGTP is better at promoting H2A-H2B deposition than either Nap1 or no chaperone. In nucleosome disassembly assays, Importin-9 can extract H2A-H2B from nucleosomes, while Nap1 and Importin-9•RanGTP have no effect. These data show that RanGTP influences the interaction between Importin-9 and H2A-H2B, possibly through an allosteric mechanism, to facilitate histone release for nucleosome assembly.
evaluation: The functional characterization of RanGTP's role in modulating Importin-9-H2A-H2B interactions is well-supported by multiple complementary assays (competition assays C76-C80, nucleosome assembly C81-C83, nucleosome disassembly C84-C85). The data consistently show that RanGTP binding changes the properties of the Importin-9•H2A-H2B complex, making it competent for histone deposition while preventing nucleosome disassembly. The proposal of an allosteric mechanism (C87) is reasonable given that the binding sites appear spatially separated (C88), though the exact mechanism remains to be determined. The functional significance for nucleosome assembly is clearly demonstrated (C89).

result: Importin-9 functions as both a nuclear import receptor and a histone chaperone for H2A-H2B. H2A-H2B belongs to a small category of nuclear import cargos that use surfaces of folded domains rather than extended NLS motifs to bind importins. Importin-9 binding blocks both nucleosomal DNA- and H3-H4-binding sites of H2A-H2B, with a much larger interface (1352 Å²) than known histone chaperone complexes. The mostly negatively charged Importin-9 shields the mostly positively charged histone-fold domain through diverse interactions including electrostatic, hydrophobic, and hydrogen bonds, with a notable charge reversal at Interface 3. Unlike most importin-cargo complexes, Importin-9•H2A-H2B is unlikely to be dissociated by RanGTP alone upon entering the nucleus. Instead, RanGTP forms a stable complex that modulates importin-histone interactions to facilitate histone release and nucleosome assembly. Importin-9 is not detected bound to H2A-H2B in the nucleus, suggesting dissociation occurs soon after nuclear entry, possibly through nucleosome assembly or hand-off to other chaperones.
evaluation: This comprehensive discussion integrates structural, biophysical, and functional data to support the dual role of Importin-9 as both import receptor and histone chaperone. The structural evidence for chaperone-like features is strong (C90-C102), including the large buried surface area and occlusion of nucleosomal interfaces. The comparison to other importin-cargo systems (C103-C104) provides context. The unusual behavior with RanGTP is well-documented (C105-C116). The cellular localization data (C108-C110) appropriately shows Importin-9-H2A-H2B interactions in cytoplasm but not nucleus. The acknowledgment of remaining questions about the exact mechanism of histone release in cells (C117-C119) is appropriate and honest about limitations.

result: Background and context: Kap114 is the S. cerevisiae homolog of human Importin-9 and the major H2A-H2B importer in yeast, with Kap121 and Kap123 as secondary importers. Importin-9 was previously shown to bind and import H2A-H2B in human cells and localizes mostly to the cytoplasm in HeLa cells. Nucleosomes are assembled in the nucleus during S-phase from newly synthesized histones that are imported by importins despite their small size. Core histones contain disordered N-terminal tails (and C-terminal tail for H2A) followed by small histone-fold domains. While histone tails contain basic residues resembling NLS motifs and can target heterologous proteins to the nucleus, removal of tails does not abolish H2A-H2B nuclear localization. Previous analysis suggested that importin-binding specificities reside not only in tail 'NLSs' but also in histone folds and bound chaperones.
evaluation: These background claims are well-supported by appropriate citations to the literature (C120-C145). The manuscript appropriately cites prior work on yeast importers (C121, C137), human Importin-9 (C122, C138), multiple backup importin systems (C139), histone structure (C140-C141), and the complexity of importin-histone recognition (C145). The cellular localization of Importin-9 is supported by both the authors' microscopy data and the Human Protein Atlas (C123-C124). The co-immunoprecipitation data confirms Importin-9-H2A-H2B interactions in the cytoplasmic fraction (C127).

result: The dissociation constant (KD) of human Importin-9 binding to full-length X. laevis H2A-H2B is 30 nM, measured by isothermal titration calorimetry.
evaluation: This binding affinity measurement is well-supported by ITC experiments performed in triplicate with appropriate error analysis (68.3% confidence interval [10, 70] nM reported in Table 1). The high affinity (30 nM) is consistent with a physiologically relevant interaction and appropriate for the crystallization conditions used.
